name: Java

modules.title: Syntax Basics, Variables & Data Types

pages.title: Core concept & syntax
pages.markdown:
## Every Java Program Starts With a Class

Java is a class-based, object-oriented language: there is no such thing as a
free-floating statement outside of a class. Every executable program needs
exactly one entry point method with this exact signature:

```java
public class Main {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        System.out.println("Hello, Java!");
    }
}
```

- **`public`** — the method is visible from outside the class (the JVM launcher needs to call it).
- **`static`** — it belongs to the class itself, not to an instance, so the JVM can invoke it without first constructing a `Main` object.
- **`void`** — it returns nothing.
- **`String[] args`** — command-line arguments are passed in as an array of strings.

## Declaring Variables

Java is **statically typed**: every variable is declared with a fixed type,
checked at compile time. You cannot later assign a `String` to a variable
declared as `int`.

```java
int age = 36;
double height = 1.7;
boolean isProgrammer = true;
char grade = 'A';
String name = "Ada";
```

Notice the type comes *before* the variable name, unlike Python or
JavaScript. Since Java 10, you can also use `var` for **local type
inference** — the compiler still assigns a concrete, fixed type, it just
figures it out from the right-hand side instead of you spelling it out:

```java
var count = 10;        // inferred as int
var label = "score";   // inferred as String
```

`var` only works for local variables with an initializer — it cannot be used
for fields, method parameters, or return types.

## Primitives vs. Reference Types

Java has exactly eight **primitive types** that hold raw values directly:
`byte`, `short`, `int`, `long`, `float`, `double`, `boolean`, and `char`.
Everything else — `String`, arrays, and any class you write — is a
**reference type**: the variable holds a reference (essentially an address)
to an object that lives on the heap.

```java
int x = 5;              // x directly contains the bits for 5
String s = "hello";     // s holds a reference to a String object on the heap
```

This distinction drives almost everything about how Java behaves — from
method parameter passing to equality comparisons — and it's worth
internalizing early.

## Comments and Statement Structure

Statements always end with a semicolon, and blocks are delimited with curly
braces `{}`. Java supports `// single-line`, `/* multi-line */`, and
`/** Javadoc */` comments, the last of which can be turned into HTML API
documentation by the `javadoc` tool.

pages.title: Deeper mechanics & nuances
pages.markdown:
## The Eight Primitives, Precisely

Each primitive has a fixed, platform-independent bit width — this is one of
Java's defining design decisions (unlike C, where `int` size varies by
platform):

| Type      | Size    | Range / notes                          |
|-----------|---------|-----------------------------------------|
| `byte`    | 8 bits  | -128 to 127                             |
| `short`   | 16 bits | -32,768 to 32,767                       |
| `int`     | 32 bits | ~-2.1 billion to 2.1 billion             |
| `long`    | 64 bits | needs an `L` suffix for large literals  |
| `float`   | 32 bits | needs an `f` suffix, single precision   |
| `double`  | 64 bits | default for decimal literals            |
| `boolean` | JVM-dependent | `true` or `false` only, not an int  |
| `char`    | 16 bits | a single UTF-16 code unit                |

```java
long bigNumber = 10_000_000_000L;   // L suffix required — literal overflows int
float pi32 = 3.14f;                 // f suffix required, else it's a double
char letter = 'A';                  // single quotes, exactly one character
int code = letter;                  // 65 — char widens to int implicitly
```

Note the **underscore digit separator** (`10_000_000_000L`) — purely
cosmetic, ignored by the compiler, but very handy for readability in large
literals.

## Where Variables Actually Live

Local variables (declared inside a method) live on the **thread's stack** —
fast, automatically reclaimed when the method returns. Object fields live
inside the object itself, on the **heap**, and stick around as long as
something references the object.

```java
public class Main {
    static int counter;              // static field: lives with the class, one copy total
    int instanceId;                  // instance field: one copy per object, on the heap

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        int local = 42;              // lives on the stack frame for main()
    }
}
```

## Default Values Exist — But Only for Fields

Uninitialized **fields** (instance or static) are automatically zeroed out by
the JVM: numeric primitives default to `0`/`0.0`, `boolean` to `false`,
`char` to `'\u0000'`, and any reference type to `null`. **Local variables**
get no such default — the compiler flatly refuses to compile code that reads
a local variable before it has been definitely assigned.

```java
public class Widget {
    int count;         // defaults to 0 automatically
    String label;      // defaults to null automatically

    void show() {
        int x;
        // System.out.println(x); // compile error: variable x might not have been initialized
    }
}
```

## String Is Not a Primitive

Even though string literals look primitive-like (`"hello"`), `String` is a
full reference type — an immutable object backed by a `char[]`/byte array
internally. The JVM interns string *literals* in a special **string pool**,
so two identical literals often refer to the same object — a detail that
matters once you start comparing strings with `==` versus `.equals()`
(covered in the next module).

pages.title: Idioms, patterns & common pitfalls
pages.markdown:
## Naming Conventions Are Not Optional in Practice

Java's ecosystem enforces naming conventions so strongly that violating them
makes code look instantly foreign to any Java developer:

- **Classes**: `PascalCase` — `BankAccount`, `HttpClient`.
- **Methods and variables**: `camelCase` — `calculateTotal`, `userName`.
- **Constants** (`static final`): `SCREAMING_SNAKE_CASE` — `MAX_RETRIES`.
- **Packages**: all lowercase, reverse-domain style — `com.codepath.app`.

```java
public class BankAccount {
    static final double MAX_OVERDRAFT = -500.0;
    private double currentBalance;

    public double getCurrentBalance() {
        return currentBalance;
    }
}
```

## Prefer `final` for Things That Don't Change

Marking a local variable or field `final` prevents reassignment and
communicates intent — many experienced Java developers make every variable
`final` by default and only drop it when mutation is truly needed.

```java
final int maxAttempts = 3;   // compiler enforces this never changes
// maxAttempts = 4;          // compile error
```

For fields, `static final` is how Java expresses a true constant.

## Common Pitfall: Confusing `float`/`double` With Exact Decimals

Floating-point types cannot represent most decimal fractions exactly, which
surprises newcomers:

```java
System.out.println(0.1 + 0.2);   // prints 0.30000000000000004, not 0.3
```

For money or anything requiring exact decimal arithmetic, use
`java.math.BigDecimal` instead of `double`.

## Common Pitfall: `char` Arithmetic Silently Becomes `int`

```java
char c = 'a';
char next = c + 1;        // compile error! c + 1 is promoted to int
char fixed = (char) (c + 1); // 'b' — needs an explicit cast back to char
```

Any arithmetic on `byte`, `short`, or `char` promotes the result to `int`,
so re-assigning back into the smaller type requires an explicit cast.

## Common Pitfall: Forgetting Suffixes on Literals

```java
long total = 5_000_000_000;   // compile error: literal itself is out of int range
long fixed = 5_000_000_000L;  // correct: L makes it a long literal

double price = 19.99;
float discount = 19.99;       // compile error: 19.99 is a double literal
float ok = 19.99f;            // correct
```

## Idiom: Group Related Declarations, One Variable Per Line

While Java allows `int a = 1, b = 2;`, most style guides (including Google's
and the one enforced by most linters) prefer one declaration per line for
readability, reserving comma-lists for tightly related loop counters.

modules.title: Operators, Expressions & Type Conversion

pages.title: Core concept & syntax
pages.markdown:
## Arithmetic, Relational & Logical Operators

Java supports the standard operator families you'd expect from any
C-family language:

- **Arithmetic**: `+ - * / % ++ --`
- **Relational**: `== != < > <= >=`
- **Logical**: `&& || !`
- **Assignment**: `= += -= *= /= %=`

```java
int a = 7, b = 2;
System.out.println(a + b);   // 9
System.out.println(a % b);   // 1 (remainder)
System.out.println(a > b);   // true

boolean loggedIn = true, isAdmin = false;
System.out.println(loggedIn && isAdmin);  // false
System.out.println(loggedIn || isAdmin);  // true
```

## Integer Division Truncates

A very common surprise for newcomers: dividing two integers always produces
an integer result, truncated toward zero — it never rounds.

```java
System.out.println(7 / 2);    // 3, not 3.5
System.out.println(-7 / 2);   // -3, truncated toward zero, not -4
```

To get a fractional result, at least one operand must be a floating-point
type:

```java
System.out.println((double) 7 / 2);  // 3.5
System.out.println(7 / 2.0);         // 3.5 — the 2.0 literal is already a double
```

## Type Conversion: Widening vs. Narrowing

**Widening** conversions (small type → bigger type) happen automatically
because no information can be lost: `byte → short → int → long → float →
double`.

```java
int i = 100;
long l = i;      // automatic widening
double d = l;    // automatic widening
```

**Narrowing** conversions (bigger type → smaller type) require an explicit
**cast**, and can lose information:

```java
double pi = 3.99;
int truncated = (int) pi;    // 3 — decimal part is simply dropped, not rounded
long big = 300L;
byte overflowed = (byte) big; // wraps around using modular arithmetic, not an error
```

## Increment/Decrement and Compound Assignment

`++x` (pre-increment) and `x++` (post-increment) both add one, but differ in
the *value of the expression itself*:

```java
int x = 5;
int a = x++;   // a = 5, then x becomes 6
int y = 5;
int b = ++y;   // y becomes 6 first, then b = 6
```

Compound assignment operators like `+=` also perform an implicit narrowing
cast, which is a subtle but useful shortcut: `byte b = 10; b += 5;` compiles
even though `b + 5` alone would be an `int`.

pages.title: Deeper mechanics & nuances
pages.markdown:
## Short-Circuit vs. Non-Short-Circuit Logical Operators

`&&` and `||` are **short-circuiting**: the right-hand operand is not
evaluated if the result is already determined by the left-hand one. `&` and
`|` also work on booleans, but they are **not** short-circuiting — both
sides always evaluate.

```java
int[] arr = {};
if (arr.length > 0 && arr[0] == 1) {   // safe: arr[0] never evaluated when length is 0
    System.out.println("first is 1");
}

if (arr.length > 0 & arr[0] == 1) {    // DANGEROUS: arr[0] evaluates even when length is 0
    // would throw ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException on an empty array
}
```

This matters whenever the right-hand side has a side effect or could throw —
always prefer `&&`/`||` unless you specifically need both sides evaluated
(e.g., to force execution of a side-effecting method on both operands).

## Autoboxing and Unboxing

Every primitive has a corresponding **wrapper class**: `int` ↔ `Integer`,
`double` ↔ `Double`, `boolean` ↔ `Boolean`, and so on. Java automatically
converts between them where needed — this is called **autoboxing**
(primitive → wrapper) and **unboxing** (wrapper → primitive).

```java
List<Integer> scores = new ArrayList<>();
scores.add(95);            // autoboxing: int 95 -> Integer.valueOf(95)
int first = scores.get(0); // unboxing: Integer -> int
```

Autoboxing is convenient, but it has real costs and pitfalls:

- **Performance**: boxed values are heap-allocated objects, not raw stack
  values — significant in tight loops or large collections.
- **`NullPointerException` risk**: unboxing a `null` wrapper throws an NPE.

```java
Integer count = null;
int x = count; // throws NullPointerException at unboxing time
```

- **Reference equality surprise**: the `Integer` cache (`-128` to `127`) means
  small boxed values compare equal with `==`, but larger ones don't:

```java
Integer a = 100, b = 100;
System.out.println(a == b);  // true — both hit the Integer cache

Integer c = 200, d = 200;
System.out.println(c == d);  // false — outside the cache, different objects!
System.out.println(c.equals(d)); // true — always compare wrapper objects with equals()
```

## `==` on Reference Types Compares Identity, Not Content

For any reference type — including `String` — `==` checks whether two
variables point to the *same object in memory*, not whether their contents
are equal.

```java
String a = "hello";
String b = "hello";
System.out.println(a == b);          // true — literals are interned, same pooled object

String c = new String("hello");
System.out.println(a == c);          // false — c is a distinct heap object
System.out.println(a.equals(c));     // true — content comparison
```

The rule of thumb: **always use `.equals()` for content comparison of
reference types**, and reserve `==` for primitives or deliberate identity
checks.

pages.title: Idioms, patterns & common pitfalls
pages.markdown:
## Idiom: Ternary Operator for Simple Conditionals

The ternary operator `condition ? valueIfTrue : valueIfFalse` is idiomatic
for short, simple assignments — but experienced developers avoid nesting it
deeply, since that quickly becomes unreadable.

```java
int age = 20;
String category = age >= 18 ? "adult" : "minor";  // clear, one condition

// Avoid: nested ternaries are hard to read
// String tier = score > 90 ? "A" : score > 80 ? "B" : score > 70 ? "C" : "F";
```

## Idiom: `Objects.equals` for Null-Safe Comparison

Comparing two references that might be `null` with `.equals()` directly
risks a `NullPointerException` if the left side is `null`. The standard
library idiom is `java.util.Objects.equals`, which handles nulls safely:

```java
import java.util.Objects;

String a = null;
String b = "test";
System.out.println(Objects.equals(a, b));  // false, no exception
```

## Common Pitfall: Comparing Wrapper Types With `==`

As shown above, `Integer`, `Long`, `Double` etc. should be compared with
`.equals()`, not `==` — the small-integer cache makes `==` *appear* to work
for values like `1` or `42`, which lulls developers into a false sense of
safety until a larger value breaks it in production.

```java
Integer x = 1000, y = 1000;
if (x == y) { /* never true here — silent bug */ }
if (x.equals(y)) { /* correct */ }
```

## Common Pitfall: Overflow Is Silent

Java integer arithmetic does **not** throw on overflow — it silently wraps
around using two's-complement arithmetic.

```java
int max = Integer.MAX_VALUE;
System.out.println(max + 1);  // -2147483648, not an exception!
```

If you need overflow-safe arithmetic, use `Math.addExact`,
`Math.multiplyExact`, etc., which throw `ArithmeticException` on overflow,
or switch to `long`/`BigInteger` for very large values.

## Common Pitfall: Mixing `float`/`double` in Equality Checks

Never compare floating-point values with `==` for "equality" after
arithmetic — rounding error makes exact equality unreliable. Compare against
a small epsilon instead:

```java
double result = 0.1 + 0.2;
System.out.println(result == 0.3);              // false!
System.out.println(Math.abs(result - 0.3) < 1e-9); // true — correct approach
```

modules.title: Methods, Parameters & Scope

pages.title: Core concept & syntax
Deeper mechanics & nuances
pages.markdown:
## The Call Stack and Stack Frames

Every method call pushes a new **stack frame** onto the current thread's
call stack, holding that invocation's parameters and local variables. When
the method returns, its frame is popped and those locals disappear. This is
why local variables from a finished method call can never "leak" into
another — and why deep, unbounded recursion eventually throws
`StackOverflowError`.

```java
static long factorial(int n) {
    if (n <= 1) return 1;
    return n * factorial(n - 1);  // each call gets its own stack frame
}
```

```java
static void recurseForever(int n) {
    recurseForever(n + 1); // no base case — will exhaust the stack
}
// recurseForever(0); // eventually throws StackOverflowError
```

## Varargs

A method can accept a variable number of arguments of the same type using
`...` (varargs), which is internally just an array:

```java
static int sum(int... numbers) {
    int total = 0;
    for (int n : numbers) {
        total += n;
    }
    return total;
}

sum();              // 0 — varargs can be called with zero arguments
sum(1, 2, 3);       // 6
sum(new int[]{4, 5}); // 9 — an actual array also works
```

A varargs parameter must be the **last** parameter in the list, and a
method can have at most one.

## Overload Resolution Nuances

When multiple overloads could apply, Java picks the **most specific**
match, preferring exact type matches, then widening primitive conversions,
then autoboxing, then varargs — in that order of preference:

```java
static void show(int x) { System.out.println("int"); }
static void show(long x) { System.out.println("long"); }
static void show(Integer x) { System.out.println("Integer (boxed)"); }
static void show(Object x) { System.out.println("Object"); }

show(5); // prints "int" — exact primitive match wins over widening/boxing
```

This ordering explains why adding an overload for a "close enough" type can
silently change which method existing calls resolve to — a subtle source
of behavior changes when a codebase evolves.

## Recursion vs. Iteration

Recursion (a method calling itself) is elegant for naturally recursive
problems (tree traversal, divide-and-conquer) but has a real memory cost —
each call retains its own stack frame until it returns. Java does **not**
guarantee tail-call optimization, so deeply recursive algorithms (like a
naive Fibonacci without memoization) should often be rewritten iteratively
or with memoization for production use.

Java is always pass-by-value; for objects, that value is a reference copy — mutation is visible, reassignment is not.

Varargs (Type... name) let a method take a variable number of arguments and must be the last parameter.

modules.title: Arrays, Collections & Strings

pages.title: Core concept & syntax
pages.markdown:
## Arrays: Fixed-Size Containers

An array holds a fixed number of elements of one type, indexed from `0`.
Once created, its size can never change.

```java
int[] nums = new int[5];         // 5 zeros: [0, 0, 0, 0, 0]
nums[0] = 10;

int[] literal = {1, 2, 3, 4, 5}; // array literal, size fixed at 5
System.out.println(literal.length); // 5, a field not a method
```

## The Collections Framework

For resizable, richer data structures, Java provides the **Collections
Framework** in `java.util`, built around **generics** (`<T>`) for
compile-time type safety:

```java
import java.util.*;

List<String> names = new ArrayList<>();   // ordered, allows duplicates, resizable
names.add("Ada");
names.add("Grace");

Set<String> unique = new HashSet<>();     // no duplicates, no guaranteed order
unique.add("red");
unique.add("red");                        // ignored, already present

Map<String, Integer> ages = new HashMap<>(); // key -> value pairs
ages.put("Ada", 36);
ages.put("Grace", 85);
System.out.println(ages.get("Ada"));      // 36
```

The three core interfaces to know: **`List`** (ordered, index-accessible,
`ArrayList` is the go-to implementation), **`Set`** (no duplicates,
`HashSet`/`LinkedHashSet`/`TreeSet`), and **`Map`** (key-value pairs,
`HashMap`/`LinkedHashMap`/`TreeMap`).

## Generics: Type Safety at Compile Time

Generics let a class or method operate on a type parameter rather than a
concrete type, catching type errors at compile time instead of at runtime
with a `ClassCastException`.

```java
List<String> strings = new ArrayList<>();
strings.add("hello");
// strings.add(42);          // compile error: incompatible types

String first = strings.get(0); // no cast needed — the compiler knows it's a String
```

## Strings Are Immutable

Once created, a `String`'s characters can never change — every "modifying"
method (`.toUpperCase()`, `.substring()`, `.replace()`, `.trim()`) returns a
**new** `String` rather than altering the original.

```java
String s = "hello";
s.toUpperCase();              // return value discarded — s is unchanged!
System.out.println(s);        // still "hello"

String upper = s.toUpperCase(); // must capture the returned value
System.out.println(upper);      // "HELLO"
```

For building strings via many small appends, use the mutable
`StringBuilder` instead, covered next.

pages.title: Deeper mechanics & nuances
pages.markdown:
## Why Repeated `String` Concatenation Is Costly

Because `String` is immutable, every `+` concatenation in a loop creates an
entirely new `String` object, copying all previous characters each time —
an O(n²) pattern for building a string of length n across n iterations.
`StringBuilder` mutates an internal buffer in place instead:

```java
StringBuilder sb = new StringBuilder();
for (int i = 0; i < 5; i++) {
    sb.append(i).append(",");
}
System.out.println(sb.toString()); // "0,1,2,3,4,"
```

`StringBuilder` also supports `.insert()`, `.delete()`, `.reverse()`, and
`.charAt()` for in-place mutation before the final `.toString()` call.

## `HashMap`/`HashSet` Rely on `hashCode()` and `equals()`

`HashMap` and `HashSet` locate elements using the key's `hashCode()` to pick
a bucket, then `equals()` to confirm an exact match within that bucket. If
you use a custom class as a key or set element without overriding both
methods consistently, lookups silently fail even for "equal" objects:

```java
class Point {
    int x, y;
    Point(int x, int y) { this.x = x; this.y = y; }
    // No equals()/hashCode() override — uses Object's identity-based defaults!
}

Set<Point> points = new HashSet<>();
points.add(new Point(1, 2));
System.out.println(points.contains(new Point(1, 2))); // false! different object identity
```

The fix is to override both consistently (an IDE or `record` — covered in
the OOP module — can generate this automatically).

## Lambdas and the Stream API

Since Java 8, functional-style operations over collections use **lambda
expressions** and the **Stream API**. A stream is a pipeline: a source, zero
or more intermediate operations (`map`, `filter`, `sorted`), and one
terminal operation (`collect`, `forEach`, `reduce`) that actually triggers
evaluation.

```java
import java.util.List;
import java.util.stream.Collectors;

List<String> names = List.of("Ada", "Grace", "Alan", "Barbara");

List<String> shortUpperNames = names.stream()
        .filter(n -> n.length() <= 4)      // lambda: keep names of length <= 4
        .map(String::toUpperCase)           // method reference, equivalent to n -> n.toUpperCase()
        .sorted()
        .collect(Collectors.toList());

System.out.println(shortUpperNames);        // [ADA, ALAN]

long count = names.stream().filter(n -> n.startsWith("A")).count();
System.out.println(count);                  // 3
```

Streams are **lazy**: intermediate operations don't run until a terminal
operation is invoked, and a stream can only be consumed once.

## Iteration Order Guarantees Differ by Implementation

`ArrayList` preserves insertion order; `HashMap`/`HashSet` make **no**
ordering guarantee at all (their iteration order depends on hash bucket
layout and can even change between JVM runs); `LinkedHashMap`/`LinkedHashSet`
preserve insertion order; `TreeMap`/`TreeSet` iterate in sorted order.
Choosing the wrong one is a subtle, common bug when code implicitly relies
on `HashMap` "happening" to iterate in insertion order during testing.

pages.title: Idioms, patterns & common pitfalls
pages.markdown:
## Idiom: Program to the Interface, Not the Implementation

Declare variables using the collection *interface* (`List`, `Set`, `Map`)
and only mention the concrete class at construction time — this makes it
trivial to swap implementations later:

```java
List<String> names = new ArrayList<>();   // good
// ArrayList<String> names = new ArrayList<>(); // works, but less flexible
```

## Idiom: `List.of()` / Immutable Collections for Fixed Data

For data that should never change after creation, `List.of(...)`,
`Set.of(...)`, and `Map.of(...)` produce genuinely immutable collections —
attempting to mutate them throws `UnsupportedOperationException`, catching
accidental mutation bugs early:

```java
List<String> fixed = List.of("a", "b", "c");
// fixed.add("d"); // throws UnsupportedOperationException
```

## Idiom: Streams for Transformation, Loops for Side Effects

A common style guideline: use streams (`map`/`filter`/`collect`) when
**transforming** data into a new collection or value, and stick with a
plain enhanced for-loop when the goal is mostly side effects (like
printing) — `forEach` on a stream works, but a for-loop is often just as
clear and easier to debug with breakpoints:

```java
// Transformation: stream reads naturally
List<Integer> squares = List.of(1, 2, 3).stream()
        .map(n -> n * n)
        .collect(Collectors.toList());

// Side effect: a for-loop is just as clear
for (int n : squares) {
    System.out.println(n);
}
```

## Common Pitfall: Modifying a Collection While Iterating It

```java
List<Integer> nums = new ArrayList<>(List.of(1, 2, 3, 4));
for (int n : nums) {
    if (n % 2 == 0) {
        nums.remove(Integer.valueOf(n)); // throws ConcurrentModificationException
    }
}
```

The fix is to use an `Iterator`'s own `.remove()`, or (more idiomatically)
`removeIf`:

```java
nums.removeIf(n -> n % 2 == 0); // safe, idiomatic
```

## Common Pitfall: `==` on Arrays and Collections

`==` on arrays checks identity, not element-by-element content — arrays
don't override `equals()`:

```java
int[] a = {1, 2, 3};
int[] b = {1, 2, 3};
System.out.println(a == b);                       // false — different objects
System.out.println(java.util.Arrays.equals(a, b)); // true — correct content comparison
```

Collections (`List`, `Set`, `Map`) *do* override `.equals()` for content
comparison, so `List.of(1,2).equals(List.of(1,2))` correctly returns `true`
— it's specifically arrays that need `Arrays.equals`.

modules.title: Memory, References & Garbage Collection

pages.title: Core concept & syntax
pages.markdown:
## The Stack and the Heap

The JVM splits memory into two conceptual regions per running program:

- **The stack**: one per thread, holding stack frames for each active
  method call — local variables and parameters of primitive/reference type.
  Extremely fast to allocate/deallocate; automatically cleaned up when a
  method returns.
- **The heap**: one shared region for the whole JVM, holding every object
  created with `new` (including array objects and String objects). Objects
  persist until nothing references them anymore.

```java
public class Main {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        int localValue = 42;                 // lives on the stack
        String name = new String("Ada");     // the reference "name" is on the stack,
                                              // the actual String object is on the heap
    }
}
```

## References Point to Objects, They Aren't the Object

A reference-type variable holds an address pointing to a heap object, not
the object's data directly. Assigning one reference variable to another
copies the *reference* (the address), not the object — both variables then
**alias** the same underlying object.

```java
import java.util.ArrayList;
import java.util.List;

List<Integer> a = new ArrayList<>(List.of(1, 2, 3));
List<Integer> b = a;      // b now points to the SAME object as a
b.add(4);
System.out.println(a);    // [1, 2, 3, 4] — a changed too, because they're aliases
```

Primitives, by contrast, are always copied by value on assignment — there
is no aliasing between two `int` variables.

## Garbage Collection: Automatic Memory Reclamation

Java manages heap memory automatically. When no reachable reference points
to an object anymore, it becomes **garbage** — eligible for the garbage
collector (GC) to reclaim. You never call `free()`; the JVM does this work
for you in the background.

```java
public class Main {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        String temp = new String("temporary");
        temp = null;   // the original "temporary" object is now unreachable
                       // and becomes eligible for garbage collection
    }
}
```

`System.gc()` exists but is only a *hint* to the JVM — it does not force an
immediate collection, and production code should essentially never call
it.

pages.title: Deeper mechanics & nuances
pages.markdown:
## Generational Garbage Collection

Most JVM garbage collectors (including the default **G1** collector on
modern JDKs) use a **generational** strategy, based on the empirical
observation that most objects die young:

- **Young generation**: newly allocated objects start here. Frequent, fast
  "minor GC" passes reclaim short-lived objects (like loop-local temporary
  objects) quickly.
- **Old generation**: objects that survive several young-generation
  collections get **promoted** here. Collections here ("major"/"full GC")
  are less frequent but more expensive, since the old generation is
  typically much larger.

This is why creating lots of short-lived objects (e.g., temporary Strings
in a loop) is often cheaper than it sounds — young-generation collection is
highly optimized — but it's still not free, and excessive garbage still
costs CPU time.

## Reachability, Not Reference Counting

Unlike some languages that use simple reference counting, the JVM
determines garbage using **reachability** from a set of **GC roots**
(active thread stacks, static fields, JNI references). This correctly
handles **cycles**: two objects referencing each other but unreachable from
any GC root are still both collected, unlike naive reference counting which
would leak them.

```java
class Node {
    Node other;
}

Node a = new Node();
Node b = new Node();
a.other = b;
b.other = a;      // a and b reference each other

a = null;
b = null;         // now nothing outside this cycle references either —
                   // both are unreachable and both get collected, despite the cycle
```

## `Optional`: An Explicit Alternative to `null`

`null` references are a notorious source of `NullPointerException`.
`java.util.Optional<T>` is a container that may or may not hold a value,
making the *possible absence* of a value explicit in a method's return
type, forcing callers to handle it deliberately:

```java
import java.util.Optional;

static Optional<String> findUserEmail(int userId) {
    if (userId == 1) return Optional.of("ada@example.com");
    return Optional.empty();
}

public static void main(String[] args) {
    Optional<String> email = findUserEmail(2);

    String result = email.orElse("no-email@example.com");    // safe default
    System.out.println(result);

    email.ifPresent(e -> System.out.println("Found: " + e)); // only runs if present

    // Avoid calling .get() without checking first — it throws NoSuchElementException if empty
}
```

`Optional` is intended primarily as a **return type** for methods that
might have no result — it's generally discouraged as a field type or
method parameter type, where a plain nullable reference (or a proper
default value) is usually clearer.

## Memory Leaks Are Still Possible in Java

Garbage collection prevents *dangling pointers*, but it cannot prevent
**logical memory leaks** — objects that are technically still reachable
(e.g., accumulating in a static `List` or an unbounded cache) but never
actually needed again. A long-lived static collection that only ever grows
is a classic Java memory leak pattern, GC or not.

pages.title: Idioms, patterns & common pitfalls
pages.markdown:
## Idiom: Null Out References You No Longer Need (Sparingly)

For most local variables this is unnecessary — they go out of scope
naturally when the method returns. But for long-lived structures (a static
field, or an object stored well beyond when it's needed), explicitly
clearing the reference can help the GC reclaim memory sooner:

```java
class Cache {
    private static java.util.List<byte[]> buffer = new java.util.ArrayList<>();

    static void releaseAll() {
        buffer.clear(); // drop references to all held byte[] objects so they become garbage
    }
}
```

## Idiom: Prefer `Optional.map`/`orElseGet`/`orElseThrow` Chains

Idiomatic `Optional` usage chains its functional methods rather than
calling `.isPresent()` followed by `.get()` (which just re-introduces the
same null-check awkwardness `Optional` was meant to avoid):

```java
import java.util.Optional;

Optional<String> raw = Optional.of("  42  ");

int value = raw
        .map(String::trim)
        .map(Integer::parseInt)
        .orElseThrow(() -> new IllegalStateException("no value present"));

System.out.println(value); // 42
```

## Common Pitfall: Calling `Optional.get()` Without Checking

```java
Optional<String> maybe = Optional.empty();
String value = maybe.get(); // throws NoSuchElementException — same class of bug as an NPE!
```

`Optional.get()` used carelessly just relocates the null-pointer-style crash
rather than preventing it. Prefer `orElse`, `orElseGet`, `orElseThrow(...)`
with a meaningful exception, or `ifPresent`.

## Common Pitfall: Believing Aliasing Bugs Are "GC Bugs"

A very common confusion: code that mutates a list through one alias and is
"surprised" the other alias also changed isn't a garbage collection issue —
it's simply two references pointing to one heap object, working exactly as
designed. Understanding aliasing (covered on the first page of this module)
resolves most of this confusion.

```java
List<Integer> original = new ArrayList<>(List.of(1, 2, 3));
List<Integer> copy = original;         // NOT a copy — still an alias!
List<Integer> trueCopy = new ArrayList<>(original); // this IS an independent copy
```

## Common Pitfall: Unbounded Caches/Static Collections

```java
class RequestLog {
    static final List<String> ALL_REQUESTS = new ArrayList<>(); // never cleared!
    static void log(String request) {
        ALL_REQUESTS.add(request); // grows forever — a slow, steady memory leak
    }
}
```

Long-lived static collections that only ever grow are the most common
"memory leak" pattern in real Java applications — the fix is a bounded
size, an expiring cache (like a `WeakHashMap` for weakly-referenced
entries), or periodic clearing.

keyTakeaways: Reference variables store a pointer to a heap object, not the object's bytes.
Assigning one reference to another aliases the same object — mutation through either is visible through both.
The garbage collector reclaims unreachable objects automatically using reachability from GC roots, not simple reference counting, so it correctly handles cycles.
Most JVMs use generational GC — a fast young generation for short-lived objects and a less frequent old generation for long-lived ones.
Primitives, by contrast, are copied by value on assignment — no aliasing between two int variables.
Optional<T> makes an absent return value explicit; chain map/orElse/orElseThrow rather than calling .get() blindly.
Garbage collection doesn't prevent logical memory leaks — unbounded static caches/collections are the classic Java leak pattern.
